lines: Last topic ended on a cliffhanger it built on purpose.
A rotation kept order intact, but nothing stopped a sorted insertion from turning the tree into one long chain. One rule fixes that, and it's colour.
Four rules about colour, layered on top of a tree that's still just a plain search tree underneath.
Search, insert, delete, none of that changes. What changes is which colours an insert is allowed to leave behind before the tree counts as valid.
Here's an insert that just landed as a red node, directly under another red node.
Before you see the fix, think about what kind of repair this actually calls for.
answer: A recolouring, and a rotation only if recolouring alone can't finish the job.
Nothing about the search tree property broke here. A separate rule did, and it has its own separate fix.

lines: Recolouring is the cheap move, and it's tried first — flip colours going back up toward the root.
When that alone can't restore the rule, one rotation finishes it. The same move from last topic, now firing for an actual reason.
Here's the part that makes the colour rule feel less arbitrary.
A black node together with its red children isn't really several separate nodes. Redraw it, and it's exactly one node of a wider, four-way tree, wearing a disguise.
Now the harder question. Across every insert and every delete this tree will ever do,
predict it: what's the largest number of rotations any single one of them can possibly need?
answer: At most two for an insert, at most three for a delete — never more, no matter what.
Every case that actually rotates happens outside the loop that walks back up fixing colours. That walk can climb a long way. The rotation at the end of it never does.

lines: Watch that play out: the recolouring climb drawn tall, as tall as the tree itself needs it to be.
And at the bottom of it, one rotation, always the same size, no matter how far the climb went to get there.
This is the piece doing the real work underneath the colour rule.
Every node of that wider four-way tree expands into at most two levels here, so this tree's height can never run away the way last topic's chain did on the exact same keys.
This isn't just a textbook exercise. Go look at the ordered map underneath the C++ standard library, and this is exactly the scheme running there.
Same story for Java's own ordered map, and for a whole list of subsystems inside the Linux kernel itself — the scheme nobody mentions until you actually go looking for it.
Everything in this topic gets checked right here, not just drawn.
Same worst-case keys from last topic, and the height stays nowhere close to that long chain.
And across every single insert and delete actually run, the rotation count never once reaches past what the source material promised.
